text: Date, commanders and outcome: Edward IV, with his brothers Gloucester and Clarence and Lord Hastings, defeated Warwick, Montagu, Oxford and Exeter. Warwick and Montagu were killed, Exeter was left for dead, Oxford escaped.
Mist: the Arrivall speaks of 'a greate myste' that stopped either side seeing the other; Warkworth independently says neither could see the other perfectly.

Misaligned lines: the Arrivall says the hosts did not meet 'directly frount to frount'. At the west end Warwick's line overreached the king's and drove it back, with many fleeing 'towards Barnet, and so forthe to London'; at the east end the king's line overreached theirs.

The night before: Edward would not let his men stay in the town, lodged them much nearer the enemy than he supposed and kept silence; Warwick's guns fired through the night and 'alway ovarshote the Kyngs hoste'.
Warwick arrived first and chose the ground; the Arrivall has his people drawn up 'undre an hedge-syde' rather more than half a mile from Barnet. Other accounts say a mile, on a 'plain'.
A chapel for the dead was built afterwards on or near the field (Great Chronicle of London, about 1512).

Survey 2015–18: systematic metal-detecting, mainly in Wrotham Park, found no clear battle scatter. A few lead round shot found earlier in the Wrotham Park, Kitts End and Old Fold area are probably from the battle. No mass grave has been found.

Army sizes. The Arrivall (the king's side) gives 9,000 against 30,000; Warkworth gives Warwick 20,000. Modern figures of about 10,000–12,000 Yorkists against about 15,000 Lancastrians (Battlefields Trust; Barnet Museum gives 10,000–13,000 and 13,000–15,000) are estimates.

The textbook deployment (Lancastrians: Oxford on the right, Montagu in the centre, Exeter on the left, Warwick in reserve; Yorkists: Hastings left, Edward centre, Gloucester right) is a modern reconstruction, not something a contemporary wrote down.
Oxford's badge of a star with streams being mistaken for Edward's sun with streams, and the cry of 'Treason': from Warkworth alone.
Casualties: Warkworth says 4,000; other figures run from about 1,000 to 10,000. None is reliable.

'Dead Man's Bottom': a name for the valley running from Bentley Heath towards Monken Mead, marked in slightly different places on 17th-century and modern maps. The report notes it may have nothing to do with the battle.
The Hadley Highstone (an obelisk of 1740, later moved) marks a traditional spot for Warwick's death; there is no evidence for it.

Where the battle was fought within a zone about 2 km long from Hadley Green to Kitts End and beyond: the survey report weighs six possible deployments and concludes that the battlefield cannot yet be identified.
The position, length and facing of both lines, and where each commander stood.
The real size of either army.
Which hedge the 'hedge-side' was, and how much of the ground was open common and how much hedged closes in 1471.
Where Warwick and Montagu died, and where the dead were buried.
The number and position of guns on either side.
How dense the mist was, and for how long; the mist shown is a rendering choice.

The only narrative source is the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 1016: Edmund 'went over at Brentford; where he fought with the enemy, and put them to flight: but there many of the English were drowned, from their own carelessness; who went before the main army with a design to plunder'.

Just before, in the same entry: Edmund gathered his force a third time, went to London 'all by north of the Thames, and so out through Clayhanger', relieved the citizens and drove the enemy to their ships. Brentford followed 'within two nights'.
Just after: Edmund went into Wessex to gather his army, and the Danes soon returned to London and attacked it by land and water.

Later in the same year Edmund, with a fourth levy, 'forded over the Thames at Brentford' and went into Kent. The Thames could therefore be waded at Brentford by an army, at least at some states of the river.

Brentford was an established, named place: recorded from 705, in connection with a meeting of the kings of Wessex and Essex, and the seat of a council under Offa in 780 and a church synod in 781. Half of a Thames fishery there was granted to Winchester in 996.

The county history judges that the lowest permanent ford on the Thames was probably at Old England, the low ground at the Brent mouth, and (citing Stenton) that the battle was fought on the south bank.

That the fight was on the Surrey bank after a crossing from north to south: an inference from the order of words in the Chronicle. A poem in praise of Cnut has been read as implying fighting on both banks (reported by Wikipedia; not checked here).
That the English dead fell in the fighting and were not drowned: argued by Frank Stenton and Russell Poole, as reported by Wikipedia (not checked here).

That the crossing was at Old England, and that timber stakes found on the foreshore there defended the ford. The stakes are undated. The older claim that they are the stakes Julius Caesar met when he forced the Thames in 54 BCE is antiquarian tradition; Mortimer Wheeler doubted it in 1929.
That Cnut was 'twice driven back across the Thames at Brentford', as a local history page puts it. The Chronicle records one fight at Brentford and one later crossing by Edmund on his way into Kent.
A Danish strength of 8,000 to 12,000, given in Wikipedia's summary box, has no contemporary basis.
The granite monument at Brentford that commemorates Caesar's crossing and the battle marks tradition, not a located site.
Where the army crossed, and on which bank or banks the fighting took place.
The day and month.
Numbers on either side, and losses. The figures in the model are stand-ins and are not to scale with any army.
Whether Cnut was there in person, and who led the Danes on the day.
Where, when and how the drowning happened: at the crossing, in pursuit, or somewhere else on the river.
The state of the tide and the river, the weather, and whether the Danes had ships at hand.
What stood at Brentford in 1016. No late Saxon building has been excavated there.
The exact form of the river: its width, the shoals and islands, and the mouths of the Brent.

Tacitus (Annals 14.33) is the only ancient writer to name Londinium in this context. He calls it a busy centre of merchants and goods, says Suetonius marched there, considered making it his base, decided to sacrifice the one town to save the province, and left; those who stayed behind were killed. Verulamium suffered the same.
Tacitus says Londinium did not have the status of a colonia. It was a trading town about a decade or so old.
There was no defence of the town: the governor abandoned it. No pitched fight at London is described in any source.

A widespread layer of burnt red clay (daub), charred wood and debris, containing pre-60 coins and samian pottery, is recorded on City sites between the Walbrook and the bridgehead. MOLA treats the 'Boudican destruction of the settlement in AD 60' as an event documented by both archaeology and text, and uses it as a dating horizon.

Burning of this date has also been found in buildings beside the Roman road at the south end of the bridge in Southwark (reported from the mid-1990s onward), so the destruction is taken to have crossed the river.
Buildings of the period were timber and clay (wattle-and-daub or mud-brick) and mostly low; burnt daub is the main component of the layer.

Recovery: a stylus tablet from the Bloomberg site records a contract dated 21 October AD 62 to bring twenty loads of provisions from Verulamium to London; a fort of about 3.7 acres with earth-and-timber ramparts and double ditches was built at Plantation Place (Fenchurch Street) in about AD 63.

Casualties: Tacitus gives 'close upon seventy thousand' Roman citizens and allies killed across the places attacked (Camulodunum, Londinium, Verulamium together, not London alone). Cassius Dio gives 80,000 and 'two cities' sacked, without naming London. Both are rhetorical round numbers; the Loeb editor's note on Tacitus calls the figure probably valueless.

Atrocities: Dio's detailed account of mutilation and impalement of captives is not tied to London and has no archaeological support. Dio survives here only in a later epitome and wrote about 150 years after the event (epitome status not verified here).
Rebel army size: Dio gives 120,000 at the outset and 230,000 at the final battle. Not usable.

Layer thickness: a secondary website gives 'typically 30-60 cm' of bright red burnt daub, with pits filled to 1.5 m; the 1928 RCHME survey records the layer at 10-13 ft below modern ground. No primary excavation figure was verified here, and the figure will vary site to site.
Population of Londinium in AD 60: modern estimates of roughly 9,000-10,000 circulate in popular accounts (seen only in search results, not verified here). There is no ancient figure.
Skulls from the Walbrook as massacre victims: an old suggestion repeated in the press; not established.
The month and season, time of day, weather, and how long the destruction took.
The direction from which the rebels approached and whether they crossed the bridge or the river to reach Southwark.
How many people remained in the town and how many died there.
Whether Boudica was present in person, and what the rebels looked like in detail.
The exact street plan and building-by-building layout of the pre-revolt town; the form of the bridge or crossing in AD 60.
Whether the whole built area burned or only parts of it; the mapped extent in Southwark.
A fortified timber bridge at London existed at this time: structural timbers are tree-ring dated to c. 987-1032, and the bridge is mentioned in the law code IV Aethelred.

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle shows the bridge mattered militarily: in 1013 part of Swein's army drowned in the Thames because they did not use a bridge, and London held out for Aethelred and Thorkell; in 1016 Cnut's ships could not pass it.
Aethelred returned in Lent 1014 and then drove Cnut out of Lindsey (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle).

Near-contemporary skaldic verse exists: Ottarr svarti's Hofudlausn, stanza 7, addresses Olaf with 'you broke the bryggjur of London'; Sigvatr Thordarson's Vikingarvisur lists a battle of Olaf's at London and Sudvirki (Southwark). These are praise poems by Olaf's own poets.
Olaf was venerated in London soon afterwards: six medieval churches in London and Southwark were dedicated to him, one at the south end of the bridge (Tooley Street is a corruption of St Olave's).

The whole narrative of the attack comes from Snorri's Heimskringla (Saga of St Olaf, written c. 1230): Danes holding London and a fortification at Southwark with large ditches and a rampart of timber, stone and turf; a bridge wide enough for two wagons to pass, with towers and breast-high wooden parapets on the downstream side, standing on piles.

The tactics are Snorri's alone: Olaf roofed his ships with platforms made from pulled-down houses (wood bound with hazel or withies, often rendered 'wattle' or 'wickerwork' in modern retellings) on stout posts, rowed up under the bridge under a hail of stones and missiles, fastened cables round the piles, and rowed hard downstream until the piles loosened and the loaded bridge gave way; Southwark was then stormed and London submitted to Aethelred.
That 'bryggjur' means the bridge: the word is plural and can mean wharves or jetties. The editor of Sigvatr's poem argues that his stanza refers to London's wharves, not its bridge.
That Olaf fought for Aethelred: this is Snorri's framing; the Encyclopaedia Romana page notes other sources put Olaf on the Danish side.
The link to the nursery rhyme 'London Bridge is falling down': Samuel Laing's 1844 translation was phrased to echo the rhyme; John Clark's study rejects the folk-memory idea.
Whether any attack on the bridge happened at all, and if so in which year and on which side Olaf fought.
Whether the bridge was pulled down, damaged, or simply fought over. Hagland and Watson, who think the attack plausible, say the damage may well be exaggerated.
The actual form of the bridge superstructure and of any Southwark defences in 1014; no excavated evidence fixes them for this date.
Numbers of ships and men, the defenders' identity, the season, weather and tide.
Whether 9th-11th-century axes, spearheads and a grappling iron dredged near the bridge relate to fighting at all (they may be carpenters' losses).

The only narrative source is the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle entry for 1016: Edmund 'went over at Brentford', fought the army and put it to flight; many English drowned through their own carelessness, having gone ahead of the main force hoping for booty.

Context in the same entry: the Danish ships came to Greenwich and then London, 'dug a great ditch on the south side and dragged their ships to the west side of the bridge', then enclosed the city with a ditch so that no one could get in or out; the city held.
The bridge was held against Cnut in 1016, which is why the ships had to be taken round it through north Southwark.
After the battle Edmund went to Wessex to gather the army and the Danes resumed the siege of London; later in the year Edmund 'forded over the Thames at Brentford' a second time on his way into Kent.
An anonymous skaldic poem, Lidsmannaflokkr, in the voice of a Danish soldier, celebrates fighting by the Thames and beside the dyke at London in this campaign (it does not describe Brentford).

That the battle was fought on the south (Surrey) bank after a crossing from north to south: an inference from the Chronicle's wording, repeated by the Victoria County History. Wikipedia reports that Knutsdrapa has been read as implying fighting on both banks (lead only, not verified here).
That the English dead were battle casualties, not drowned: argued by Frank Stenton and Russell Poole according to Wikipedia (lead only, not verified here).
That the crossing was at Old England by the Brent mouth, and that the foreshore stakes there relate to a defended ford: possible, unproven, and the stakes are undated in the source read.
The modern Brentford monument listing the battle marks tradition, not a located site.
A Danish strength of 8,000-12,000 appears in Wikipedia's infobox without contemporary basis.
The date, the exact crossing point, and which bank the fighting was on.
Whether Cnut was present in person; who commanded the Danes on the day.
Numbers on either side and losses.
Where and how the drowning happened (at the ford on the crossing, or in pursuit).
The course and width of Cnut's ditch through Southwark; no excavated trace was verified here.
The state of the tide, the weather, and the look of the riverbank (the Thames here was wider, shallower and braided with aits).

Date, commanders and outcome: Edward IV defeated Warwick; Warwick and Montagu were killed; the Duke of Exeter was badly wounded and left for dead; the Earl of Oxford escaped. Henry VI was brought to the field with Edward's army and returned to the Tower.
Mist or fog: reported independently by the Arrivall, Warkworth and Gerhard von Wesel's newsletter of 17 April 1471 (which says the fog was also in London).

Misaligned lines: the Arrivall says the two battles did not meet 'directly frount to frount' because of the mist. At the west end the Lancastrians overreached the king's line and drove it back, with fugitives fleeing through Barnet towards London; at the east end the king's line overreached theirs.
Night before: Edward would not let his men stay in the town, lodged them very close to the enemy and kept silence; Warwick's guns fired through the night and overshot.

Warwick had arrived first and chose the ground; the Arrivall has him 'undre an hedge-syde' somewhat more than half a mile from Barnet; von Wesel and the Great Chronicle of London imply nearer a mile. The battle was fought on foot.

Yorkist order of march and battle (Great Chronicle of London, Hall): Gloucester the vanguard, Edward with Clarence the main battle, Hastings the rearward. Oxford led the Lancastrian vanguard and routed the wing opposite him, which was Hastings's.
A chapel for the dead was established near the field soon after; the hermitage chapel at Kitts End is the usual candidate, but geophysics there found a moat and no graves.
Survey finds 2015-18: of 1,007 recorded objects only 16-17 were certainly medieval; a few lead round shot are known from the Wrotham Park / Kitts End / Old Fold area. No mass grave has been found.

Army sizes: the sources contradict each other along party lines. Arrivall (Yorkist): 9,000 against 30,000. Warkworth: Edward about 7,000-8,000 against Warwick 20,000. Von Wesel: Edward 15,000-20,000. Polydore Vergil (decades later): Edward 'far superior' in numbers. Modern compromise figures (Hammond: about 12,000 Yorkists, 15,000 Lancastrians; others 10,000 and 15,000) are estimates, and the project report notes historians now tend to reduce such numbers further.

The tidy textbook deployment (Lancastrians: Oxford right, Montagu centre, Exeter left, Warwick in reserve; Yorkists: Hastings left, Edward centre, Gloucester right) is a modern reconstruction. The wing positions are inferred from military convention (vanguard on the right) plus the Arrivall; Hall, the only chronicler to give a Lancastrian order, puts Oxford and Montagu on the left, Warwick and Exeter on the right, and Somerset (who was not there) in the centre.

Oxford's star badge mistaken for Edward's sun and the cry of 'Treason': from Warkworth alone. The History of Parliament notes it 'is perhaps not to be taken too seriously' and that there is no evidence a star with streams was a de Vere badge.
Montagu wearing Edward's livery and being killed by Warwick's own men (Warkworth): regarded as improbable.
Warwick killed fleeing to a wood, or while reaching his horse: details vary by source. The Hadley Highstone obelisk (1740) marks a traditional spot only.

Casualties: Sir John Paston's letter says over 1,000 besides the notables; Warkworth about 4,000; a foreign report 10,000; von Wesel says more than 10,000 broken arrows lay on the field. None is reliable.

Place-names 'Gladmore Heath' and 'Dead Man's Bottom': the project report shows 'Gladmore Heath' grew out of a map label ('Gladmore heath field') on Norden's 1598 map, and treats Dead Man's Bottom as a late, possibly spurious association.

The exact position, length and orientation of both battle lines (probably roughly east-west across or beside the St Albans road, but six different deployments are considered possible in the project report).
The real size of either army and of each division, and where Warwick, Montagu and Exeter each stood.
Where Warwick and Montagu died.
The number, type and position of guns on either side.
How far the landscape was open heath or hedged enclosure in 1471 (the commons were probably larger than later maps show).
How long the fighting lasted and how dense the mist was through the morning.
The monument's main axis runs north-east to south-west, shared by the trilithon horseshoe, the bluestone settings, the sarsen circle and the first stretch of the Avenue (Darvill et al. 2012).
Midsummer sunrise is seen over and slightly to the left of the Heel Stone and falls within the Avenue (Sky at Night).

The first straight stretch of the Avenue leaves the stones at azimuth about 49.9 degrees, measured from OpenStreetMap-mapped earthwork outlines (this project's geography research, not a survey azimuth).
William Stukeley recognised the solstice axis in 1720.
That the builders meant midsummer sunrise: Ruggles favours midwinter as the more important; Hawkins's 1960s claims are generally treated as over-optimistic.
That crowds gathered at the stones on this morning in 2500 BCE; the figures are not shown.
What, if anything, was done at the stones on midsummer morning, and whether the alignment was meant to be precise to a degree.
The altitude of the true horizon north-east of the stones (woodland, relief): the computed range uses a flat 0 degree and a 0.6 degree horizon as an assumption.
Today the same sunrise is about 1 degree larger in azimuth (49.2 degrees on a flat horizon) because the Earth's axial tilt has fallen from about 24.0 to 23.4 degrees.

Computed with cos A = (sin d - sin phi sin h) / (cos phi cos h), latitude 51.179 degrees, obliquity 23.97 degrees (Laskar series, 2500 BCE), refraction 0.57 degrees, solar semi-diameter 0.27 degrees: my calculation, not a source.
From the far end of the Avenue the midwinter sunset can be seen through the central arches (Sky at Night).
The Avenue's first straight stretch, the trilithon horseshoe and the circles share one axis, open to the north-east and facing the Great Trilithon in the south-west (Darvill et al. 2012).
Durrington Walls pig-tooth evidence points to midwinter slaughter and feasting (cited by Parker Pearson in the Sky at Night account).

That the monument was built to frame the midwinter sunset (Ruggles's preferred reading; Darvill argues the trilithon layout points to a midwinter focus). Midsummer sunrise as the main intent is the older, popular view.
That people gathered on this evening; none are drawn.
What ceremonies took place, and whether the alignment was precise to better than a degree.
The altitude of the south-west horizon, so the exact azimuth range: 230.0 to 231.0 degrees assumes a 0 to 0.6 degree horizon, my assumption.
Today the sunset is about 1 degree larger in azimuth (231.0 degrees flat horizon) than in 2500 BCE. Computed as in the sunrise episode; my calculation, not a source.
A sarsen circle of 30 uprights and 30 lintels, outer diameter about 29.6 m, was designed (Darvill et al. 2012); the uprights are about 4.1 m high, the lintel tops about 4.9 m above ground.
Five trilithons form a horseshoe about 13.7 m across, open to the north-east; the tallest stone (56) stands about 6.7 m above ground with about 2.4 m buried.
Radiocarbon dating of an antler in the socket of stones 53 and 54 gives 2585 to 2400 BCE (93%).
The sarsens come from the Marlborough Downs about 25 km north (English Heritage; Nash et al. 2020, from a search summary only).
Geoffrey of Monmouth's tale that Merlin brought the stones from Ireland (1136) is legend.
How the stones were transported and raised, how many people it took and how long it took.

Whether the sarsen circle was ever completed: stones 13, 17, 18, 20 and 24 and 24 lintels are missing today. Ashbee argued it was never finished; Darvill thinks it was robbed; parchmarks from 2013 hint at a complete circle. Unresolved.
The order of the trilithons, circle and bluestone settings within Stage 2.
Eight houses about 5 m (16 ft) square, with clay floors, central hearths and box-bed and dresser outlines, were excavated in 2006.
Occupation was brief, about 10 to 12 years, with chalk floors renewed at most nine times (Bayesian modelling).
Pig-tooth evidence points to midwinter slaughter (cited by Parker Pearson in the Sky at Night account); the Southern Circle is oriented to midwinter sunrise (Wikipedia).
Up to about 300 timber posts in a ring 440 to 450 m across stood under the later bank; they were pulled about 2480 BCE.
That Durrington's occupants were connected with building or using Stonehenge: widely suggested, not proven by the sources read.
That feasting here was tied to a midwinter gathering at Stonehenge, 'up to 4,000 people' being an upper-end speculation.
The number of houses and people (a few dozen houses are drawn, conjecturally), and exactly where in the henge they stood.
What the timber ring and the circles were for; whether the Avenue to the river was walked at this season.
The height of the posts (5 m per the 2016 excavations, 7 m per Wikipedia: conflict).
Bush Barrow lies on Normanton Down, 3.3 m high and 49 m overall (or 40 m wide by another count).
It held an Early Bronze Age burial with a gold lozenge about 184 x 156 x 1 mm, dated about 1950 BCE.
Normanton Down has about 40 round barrows (bowl, bell, disc and a saucer), of which at least 35 were surviving in 1957, with burials between about 2600 and 1600 BCE.
That the burial was a chieftain's or king's: 'chieftain' is a modern label.
That the barrows were meant to be seen from the stones, or the reverse.
The buried person's name, status or relation to Stonehenge, and the exact date of the burial.
The barrow's original form: its present shape is modern survey, and the model's 'new' mound is generic.
The other grave goods are not itemised in the research notes for this project.
A Benedictine abbey was founded at Amesbury c. 979 by Queen Aelfthryth (Wikipedia).
It was refounded as a Fontevraud priory in 1177 and dissolved c. 1540; the estate went to the Seymours.
The parish church of St Mary and St Melor may be the surviving priory church (Wikipedia; unproven).
The site, size and form of the 10th-century buildings, and the precinct's boundary.
Whether the Dissolution date is 1539 or 1540: sources conflict.
Jones surveyed Stonehenge for James I in the 1620s (English Heritage); Webb's 1655 publication reports the king's commission after his visit to Wilton in 1620.
The Duke of Buckingham's digging in the centre is the first known excavation there (English Heritage).
Stone 55 and the Great Trilithon had fallen before the first 17th-century plans (Darvill); the south-west trilithon (57 and 58 with lintel 158) stood until 1797.
Jones's claim that Stonehenge was a Roman temple: now rejected.
Which other stones were fallen, leaning or broken in 1625: no dated record; the model uses inference from later plans.
How accurately Jones measured: his plan is an ideal geometry and cannot be used as a measured survey.
A causewayed enclosure with two ditch circuits and low banks, with one causeway noted by Wikipedia.
Dated to the centuries around 3500 BCE by English Heritage.
Its diameter, internal features and the date it went out of use.
